title: World Religions · Episode 3
chapters: How the Bible became a book

units.t: World Religions. Episode three.
In this episode: Christianity, How the Bible became a book and Islam.
Part one. Christianity.
The world's largest religion began with a Jewish teacher in a small Roman province.
Two thousand years later, it shapes the calendar, laws and holidays of countries like Australia.
Jesus and his teaching.
Christianity centres on Jesus of Nazareth, a Jewish teacher in Galilee and Judea, then under Roman rule.
He was probably born around 4 BCE and was crucified in Jerusalem around 30 CE under the Roman governor Pontius Pilate.
Most historians agree he existed, taught, gathered followers and was crucified.
Christians believe more: that he is the Son of God and the Messiah, and rose from the dead three days later.
"Christ" comes from the Greek for anointed one, translating the Hebrew Messiah.
According to the Gospels, Jesus taught that people should love God with all their heart and their neighbour as themselves.
He taught through parables, such as the Good Samaritan and the Prodigal Son.
The Sermon on the Mount includes the Beatitudes and the Lord's Prayer.
He welcomed outsiders and healed the sick.
The Bible and core beliefs.
The Bible has two main parts.
The Old Testament largely matches the Hebrew Bible.
The New Testament has 27 books written in Greek, including four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, letters, many by Paul, and Revelation.
Catholic and Orthodox Bibles include some additional Old Testament books.
It has been translated into more languages than any other book.
Most Christians believe in one God who exists as a Trinity: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
They believe God became human in Jesus, the incarnation, and that through his death and resurrection people can be reconciled with God and receive eternal life, called salvation.
Many churches summarise their beliefs in the Nicene Creed, agreed in 325 CE.
Most practise baptism and Holy Communion, sharing bread and wine in memory of Jesus.
Spread and branches.
After Jesus's death, apostles such as Peter and Paul spread the message across the Roman Empire.
Early Christians were a small, sometimes persecuted minority.
Emperor Constantine legalised Christianity in 313 CE, and in 380 it became the empire's official religion.
Armenia, around 301, and the Ethiopian kingdom of Aksum, 330s, had already adopted it.
Today most Christians live outside Europe, with large growing numbers in Africa and Latin America.
In 1054, tensions between Rome and Constantinople separated the Catholic Church, led by the Pope, from the Eastern Orthodox churches.
In 1517, Martin Luther's criticisms helped spark the Protestant Reformation, producing Lutheran, Anglican, Baptist, Methodist and many other churches.
Catholics, with over a billion members, are about half of all Christians.
Christmas and Easter.
Christmas, on 25 December, celebrates the birth of Jesus.
Many Orthodox Christians celebrate on 7 January because they follow the older Julian calendar.
For Christians, Easter is the most important festival.
It is preceded by Lent, a season of about 40 days of reflection and often fasting.
Holy Week includes Good Friday, remembering Jesus's crucifixion, and ends with Easter Sunday, celebrating his resurrection.
Easter's date moves each year, falling on a Sunday between late March and late April, based on the spring full moon in the northern hemisphere.
Christianity in Australia.
Christianity arrived with the First Fleet in 1788, whose chaplain, Richard Johnson, was Anglican.
Irish convict and settler families made Catholicism a major force.
In the 2021 Census Catholics were the largest group at about 20%, followed by Anglicans at about 10%.
Overall, about 44% of Australians identified as Christian, down from much higher levels in earlier decades.
The Uniting Church formed in 1977 from Methodist, Congregational and most Presbyterian churches.
Mary MacKillop, canonised in 2010, is Australia's first saint.
Church-run schools, hospitals and charities remain significant.
The key idea: Jesus was a Jewish teacher in Roman-ruled Judea who taught love of God and neighbour; Christians believe he rose from the dead.
Part two. How the Bible became a book.
The Bible was not written at once, nor agreed on in a single meeting.
It grew over a thousand years, and Christians still do not all have the same list of books.
A library, not a book.
The word Bible comes from the Greek ta biblia, "the books".
It is a library, not a single work, holding law, history, poetry, prophecy, proverbs, letters and visions.
Most of it was written in Hebrew and Greek, with some Aramaic, over a span usually put at more than a thousand years.
A canon is the official list of books a community accepts as scripture, from a Greek word for a measuring rod.
The Jewish Bible has 24 books.
Protestant Bibles have 66, Catholic Bibles 73, and Eastern Orthodox and Oriental churches more again.
Even chapters and verses are late additions: chapters date from the thirteenth century, New Testament verse numbers from 1551.
Torah, Prophets, Writings.

Jewish scripture is called the Tanakh, an acronym of its three parts: Torah, the Teaching, the five books of Moses, Nevi'im, the Prophets, and Ketuvim, the Writings, including Psalms, Proverbs and Job.
Scholars generally think the Torah was recognised as authoritative first, probably by around the fifth or fourth century BCE, then the Prophets.
The Writings stayed open longer.
Rabbinic texts record debates over whether Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs belonged, and the list seems to have been broadly settled in the early centuries CE.
Protestant Old Testaments hold the same material, counted as 39 books rather than 24 because Samuel, Kings and the twelve minor prophets are divided differently.
Why Christian lists differ.
From the third century BCE, Greek-speaking Jews in Alexandria translated their scriptures into Greek.
A legend says seventy-two scholars finished in seventy-two days, hence the name Septuagint, from the Latin for seventy.
The Greek collections also held books outside the Jewish canon, such as Tobit, Judith, Sirach and Maccabees.
Early Christians mostly read Greek and used it widely.
Catholics call these extra books deuterocanonical, and Protestants call them the Apocrypha.
In 1534 Martin Luther placed them in a separate section, useful but not equal to scripture.
In 1546 the Council of Trent affirmed them as canonical.
Orthodox churches accept more again, and the Ethiopian Orthodox canon is largest, usually counted at around 81 books.
The Dead Sea Scrolls.
In 1947 Bedouin shepherds exploring caves near Qumran, on the north-western shore of the Dead Sea, found jars holding ancient scrolls.
Over the next decade around 900 manuscripts, mostly fragments, were recovered from eleven caves.
Dating mainly from the third century BCE to the first century CE, they include copies or fragments of every Hebrew Bible book except Esther.
Until then, the oldest complete Hebrew Bible manuscripts were medieval, such as the Leningrad Codex of about 1008 CE.
The Great Isaiah Scroll, roughly a thousand years older, proved remarkably close to the medieval text.
Other scrolls show variant versions, revealing that some books still circulated in more than one form.
Not decided at Nicaea.
Paul's letters, usually dated to the 50s CE, are the earliest New Testament writings.
Most scholars date the four gospels to roughly 70 to 100 CE.
By around 200 CE the gospels and Paul's letters were widely accepted, while Hebrews, James, 2 Peter, Jude and Revelation stayed disputed longer.
The Shepherd of Hermas was read in some churches but left out.
A popular claim, spread by novels such as The Da Vinci Code, says Constantine and the Council of Nicaea in 325 CE picked the books.
There is no evidence for it.
Nicaea dealt with the nature of Christ, the date of Easter and church discipline.
In 367 CE Athanasius wrote the earliest known list matching today's 27 books, and councils at Hippo, 393, and Carthage, 397, endorsed similar lists.
The key idea: The Bible is a library of writings from many authors, and different communities keep different official lists, called canons.
Part three. Islam.
About one in four people on Earth is Muslim.
The largest Muslim nation is not in the Middle East, and Muslims first reached Australia's shores long before the cameleers.
Faith, prophet and Qur'an.
The Arabic word Islam means submission to the will of God.
Allah is simply the Arabic word for God.
The central belief is tawhid, the oneness of God.
Muslims believe God sent many prophets, including Adam, Abraham, Ibrahim, Moses, Musa, and Jesus, Isa, and that Muhammad was the last.
Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570 CE and became a respected merchant.
Muslims believe that around 610 he received the first revelation through the angel Jibril, Gabriel.
After opposition in Mecca, he and his followers moved to Medina in 622, a journey called the Hijra that starts the Islamic calendar.
He died in 632.
The Qur'an, revealed over about 23 years, has 114 chapters, called surahs.
The Arabic original is the true Qur'an; translations are interpretations.
Many Muslims memorise it all, earning the title hafiz.
Five Pillars and Ramadan.
Muslim practice rests on five pillars.
Shahada is the declaration of faith: there is no god but God, and Muhammad is the messenger of God.
Salat is prayer five times a day, facing the Kaaba in Mecca.
Zakat is giving to those in need, commonly 2.
5% of savings above a set threshold each year.
Sawm is fasting from dawn to sunset in Ramadan.
Hajj is the pilgrimage to Mecca, which every adult Muslim who is able should make at least once.
Ramadan is the ninth month of the lunar calendar.
The lunar year is about 11 days shorter than the solar year, so Ramadan moves earlier each year.
Children, the sick, travellers and pregnant women may be exempt.
Each evening the fast is broken with a shared meal, iftar.
Eid al-Fitr, a joyful festival, ends the month.
Sunni, Shia and the world.
After Muhammad's death, his followers disagreed over who should lead.
Those who became Sunni accepted Abu Bakr, a close companion, as the first caliph.
Those who became Shia believed leadership belonged to Ali, Muhammad's cousin and son-in-law, and his descendants.
Shia Muslims mourn the death of Ali's son Husayn at Karbala in 680 each year at Ashura.
Today about 85 to 90% of Muslims are Sunni and 10 to 15% Shia, the majority in Iran and Iraq.
Sufism, a mystical tradition, is found within both.
Only about one in five Muslims is Arab.
Indonesia has the largest Muslim population of any country, followed by Pakistan, India and Bangladesh.
Science and learning.
From about the eighth to the thirteenth centuries, scholars in the Islamic world made major advances.
In Baghdad, the House of Wisdom gathered and translated Greek, Persian and Indian works.
Al-Khwarizmi wrote a founding text on algebra, a word that comes from Arabic, and his name gave us "algorithm".
Ibn al-Haytham used experiments to study light and vision.
Ibn Sina's Canon of Medicine was taught in European universities for centuries.
The numerals we use today, first developed in India, reached Europe largely through Arabic texts, and many stars still carry Arabic names.
Islam in Australia.
Contact with Australia is old.
From at least the 1700s, Makassan sailors from Sulawesi, many of them Muslim, visited northern Australia to harvest trepang, or sea cucumber, trading with the Yolngu of Arnhem Land.
From the 1860s, cameleers, known as Afghans though many came from British India, opened up the outback and built some of Australia's first mosques.
The Ghan train is named after them.
At the 2021 Census, about 3% of Australians were Muslim.
The key idea: Islam means submission to the one God, and Muslims believe the Qur'an was revealed to the Prophet Muhammad.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What do most historians agree about Jesus?
Answer. He lived, taught and was crucified.
Question two. What is a canon of scripture?
Answer. An official list of books a community accepts.
Question three. What does the word Islam mean?
Answer. Submission to the will of God.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
